BBC Seven Worlds One Planet

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We go behind the scenes on an iconic wildlife series, and explore how David Attenborough and the BBC are using a celebration of natural wonder to inspire climate action

Unique Selling Point:
The BBC's latest natural history series launches in South Africa on 29 March 2020. Bringing the wonders of the natural world to our living rooms since the 1950s, the BBC's Natural History Unit has always been at the forefront of technological innovation and narrative drama in scientific storytelling. But both the production house and its iconic presenter, Sir David Attenborough, have long shied away from taking a stance on climate change and the destruction human beings are wreaking on the planet. Until now. This series is bigger and bolder than ever before, featuring animal behaviours never before captured on camera with brand new technology - but along with the marvels comes a message: we need to act now, or lose all this forever. We go behind the scenes on the making of a masterpiece.

Summary:
The Seven Worlds One Planet series divides the world into seven continents, with each 50 minute-long episode exploring the wonders great and small of each continent.

We will focus on the ever more urgent question of climate change and human destruction of the natural world. We will ask what the BBC's production teams experienced and uncovered in terms of the challenges species are facing around the world, and the ways they are tackling those challenges.

We will also go behind the scenes through the BBC's 'making of' clips, which show the extremes that film-makers face to bring these incredible stories to life for viewers. Some incredible ‘film firsts’ were achieved in making this series, including the largest aggregation of whales ever filmed, wolves hunting in the mountains of Italy, and multiple animal interactions captured in unprecedented detail thanks to the development of smaller, quieter drones.

We will interview series Executive Producer Jonny Keeling about the BBC's newly strengthened stance on climate change. We will hopefully also interview a crew member or producer (possibly via Skype/sent from location) about the experience of shooting such an ambitious and groundbreaking project.

We will also select one or two success stories the series tells about species brought back from the brink: whales almost hunted out, or pumas in Patagonia which are slowly recovering now that their habitat has been protected. We will hopefully interview one of the scientists involved in one of these projects, who can tell us the story of how to save a species.

The gist of the Seven Worlds One Planet series and our story will be a celebration of our natural wonders alongside an awareness of how delicate these systems are and how vital it is to preserve them.

Further information:
We will shoot at the launch of the series on Saturday 7 March 2020, capturing links, an interview with EP Jonny Keeling and some visuals of guests arriving to watch the Africa episode (series finale).

The other interviews are yet to be set up and will happen at a later date.

In conversation with BBC it has been agreed that the insert will TX on 22 March 2020, one week before the launch of the series.

Press Release:


David Attenborough’s new blockbuster series “Seven Worlds, One Planet” features brand new animal behaviours and cutting-edge technology, underpinned by an urgent message to take better care of the earth. From poaching to habitat loss and climate change – the world as we know it is under threat. Carte Blanche previews this phenomenal series that features breath-taking footage from every continent and takes wildlife storytelling to new levels.

Script:


CLIP (Seven Worlds: Antarctica On Location): Cameraman: If you fall in the water here, there’s nothing anyone can do. They can’t save you. It’s so cold you’ll die in under a couple of minutes. Wow!
VO1: This camera crew is on its way to St Andrew’s Bay in the Antarctic. It’s a 10-day journey across the world’s roughest seas.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: Antarctica On Location): [vomiting] Cameraman: The last week on this boat has been probably one of the worst experiences of my life so far.
VO2: Working in the field for the BBC Natural History Unit is no walk in the park, says executive producer Jonny Keeling.
UPSOUND: Jonny Keeling: We definitely had some moments of danger. But you can only really be afraid for about 20 seconds and then you have to just cope with it.
VO3: But what such adversity produces is this: breath-taking footage of the planet’s most iconic species – and some of its least known.
LINK1: We’re here to celebrate the launch of David Attenborough’s most recent spectacular, Seven Worlds, One Planet.
VO4: It’s a seven-part blockbuster showcasing the geography and biodiversity that makes each of our continents unique.
In his long career, Attenborough has seen this genre transformed beyond recognition. Today, technology brings us closer to the wild than ever before.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: North America): David Attenborough: On a few special nights, when the temperature is just right, the forests of North America put on a show.
VO5: Cameras gliding on cables strung between the trees bring this fairy-tale dance of fireflies to life.
UPSOUND: Jonny Keeling: We decided to do a sort of tracking time lapse through the forest, through the night. You start out thinking well it's probably going to work. And it comes back and it's 10 times better than you imagined.
VO6: Advanced thermal imaging cameras designed by the British military capture one of the world’s most elusive predators in Italy.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: Europe): David Attenborough: Wolves. Right on the edge of the village.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: Europe On Location): Camerawoman: We’ve got nine European wild wolves howling down there in the valley. Unbelievable.
UPSOUND: Jonny Keeling: No one's filmed them hunting here before. I'm not sure whether wolves have been filmed hunting in Europe at all. Certainly not at night.
VO7: And with the help of drones, unique behaviours are caught on camera for the very first time.
All this is a far cry from Attenborough’s early days.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: Asia On Location): David Attenborough: And high up in the trees, we saw a great furry red form.
LINK2: A lot has changed in the six decades since David Attenborough began his career at the BBC, and it’s not just the technology. Even as the phrase “climate change” becomes something of a cliché, the human destruction of the natural world is at a crisis point.
VO8: Since Attenborough’s first trip to Borneo in 1956, the orangutan population has more than halved. Today, they survive in isolated pockets of forest. The picture is dismally similar across the planet.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: South America): David Attenborough: Over 95% of Colombia’s lowland forest has now been cleared. Throughout South America as a whole, an area the size of a football pitch is being lost every five seconds.
VO9: And beyond habitat loss and poaching, an even bigger threat is looming.
LINK3: The planet is warming, and we are experiencing extreme weather events around the world. And animals that have adapted to harsh conditions over millions of years are being pushed beyond the edge.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: Antarctica On Location): Director: Thirty years ago, the front of that glacier was right down on the beach. It’s retreated a huge amount. And I don’t really know what climate change is going to mean for all the wildlife that’s living here.
UPSOUND: Jonny Keeling: I think you can't tell a story about Antarctica without at least touching on climate change. And you can't really tell a story about South America if you're not ever referencing deforestation. We can't shy away from the fact that there is a loss of biodiversity and it's happened dramatically, in a single human lifetime.
VO10: For some species, it may already be too late. Others are carving out a niche right under our noses.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: Europe): David Attenborough: Wild hamsters are found in grasslands throughout central Europe. Here in the city, they’re doing extremely well.
UPSOUND: Derek Watts: Why did you make the decision to show more manmade structures and humans were evident?
Jonny Keeling: Well we're documenting the natural world, so the natural world now has a lot of humans in it, 7 billion of us. And some of those stories are fascinating: how are animals coping in a manmade world?
VO11: Some species are adapting to changing conditions. In drought-stricken Zimbabwe, a few elephants have learned to reach foliage high above the ground.
LINK4: Is there any glimmer of hope? Can we change the fate of these imperilled species? This series seems to suggest that we can.
VO12: In Antarctica, whales are returning from the very brink of extinction. Over one and a half million were slaughtered here before commercial hunting was banned in 1986.
UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: It's a sign for how, if humans really take care to protect the environment then great things can happen.
VO13: Dr Jennifer Jackson researches recovering whale populations and advised the Seven Worlds Antarctica team.
UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: We use satellite tags to follow whales. And those tags then send transmissions about where the whales are to a satellite so we can find out where they are in real time. We also use drones. We can identify how healthy they are by looking at how fat they are. We can also breathalyse whales by getting a sample of the blow and looking at their bacterial health.
VO14: And the BBC crew was lucky enough to capture this sign of the whales’ recovery.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: Antarctica): David Attenborough: On the horizon, over 150 whales have gathered to feast on krill. This is the largest congregation of great whales ever filmed.
UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: It's a privilege to be able to see so many whales together in the wild again. And I think a lot of it is down to really good habitat protection.
VO15: Of course, the battle is not yet won.
UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: It's hard to see the impact of climate change yet. But what we do know is that in many oceans, whales are impacted by our shipping. They're impacted by pollution and they're impacted by entanglement in our fishing nets.
VO16: But there is hope that this success can be repeated elsewhere.
UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: It takes people really caring about the environment. If people felt that inspiration and took it seriously, I think we would be able to reverse a lot of the damaging declines that we've wrought.
UPSOUND: Jonny Keeling: I want people to go away at the end feeling like they've fallen in love with the natural world and they really want to protect it.
Derek Watts: And it's not saying that we are doomed.
Jonny Keeling: No, quite the opposite. We show examples of animals doing well when people have made an effort and we're trying to give people hope.
CLIP (Seven Worlds: Africa): David Attenborough: This is a crucial moment in time. The decisions we take now will influence the future of animals, humanity and indeed, all life on earth.

PROMOS

1. VO: David Attenborough’s Seven Worlds, One Planet features new species and cutting-edge technology. But there’s also a growing urgency: this world is under threat.

2. VO: From habitat loss to climate change – the natural world is under threat. But can we act in time to make a difference? This new series says we can.

3. VO: From the oceans of Antarctica to the plains of Africa, a new blockbuster series brings the wonders of the natural world closer than ever before.

UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: It's a sign for how, if humans really take care to protect the environment then great things can happen. VO13: Dr Jennifer Jackson researches recovering whale populations and advised the Seven Worlds Antarctica team. UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: We use satellite tags to follow whales. And those tags then send transmissions about where the whales are to a satellite so we can find out where they are in real time. We also use drones. We can identify how healthy they are by looking at how fat they are. We can also breathalyse whales by getting a sample of the blow and looking at their bacterial health. VO14: And the BBC crew was lucky enough to capture this sign of the whales’ recovery. CLIP (Seven Worlds: Antarctica): David Attenborough: On the horizon, over 150 whales have gathered to feast on krill. This is the largest congregation of great whales ever filmed. UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: It's a privilege to be able to see so many whales together in the wild again. And I think a lot of it is down to really good habitat protection. VO15: Of course, the battle is not yet won. UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: It's hard to see the impact of climate change yet. But what we do know is that in many oceans, whales are impacted by our shipping. They're impacted by pollution and they're impacted by entanglement in our fishing nets. VO16: But there is hope that this success can be repeated elsewhere. UPSOUND: Jennifer Jackson: It takes people really caring about the environment. If people felt that inspiration and took it seriously, I think we would be able to reverse a lot of the damaging declines that we've wrought. UPSOUND: Jonny Keeling: I want people to go away at the end feeling like they've fallen in love with the natural world and they really want to protect it. Derek Watts: And it's not saying that we are doomed. Jonny Keeling: No, quite the opposite. We show examples of animals doing well when people have made an effort and we're trying to give people hope. CLIP (Seven Worlds: Africa): David Attenborough: This is a crucial moment in time. The decisions we take now will influence the future of animals, humanity and indeed, all life on earth. PROMOS 1. VO: David Attenborough’s Seven Worlds, One Planet features new species and cutting-edge technology. But there’s also a growing urgency: this world is under threat. 2. VO: From habitat loss to climate change – the natural world is under threat. But can we act in time to make a difference? This new series says we can. 3. VO: From the oceans of Antarctica to the plains of Africa, a new blockbuster series brings the wonders of the natural world closer than ever before.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We go behind the scenes on an iconic wildlife series, and explore how David Attenborough and the BBC are using a celebration of natural wonder to inspire climate action
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The BBC's latest natural history series launches in South Africa on 29 March 2020. Bringing the wonders of the natural world to our living rooms since the 1950s, the BBC's Natural History Unit has always been at the forefront of technological innovation and narrative drama in scientific storytelling. But both the production house and its iconic presenter, Sir David Attenborough, have long shied away from taking a stance on climate change and the destruction human beings are wreaking on the planet. Until now. This series is bigger and bolder than ever before, featuring animal behaviours never before captured on camera with brand new technology - but along with the marvels comes a message: we need to act now, or lose all this forever. We go behind the scenes on the making of a masterpiece.
metadata.Summary: The Seven Worlds One Planet series divides the world into seven continents, with each 50 minute-long episode exploring the wonders great and small of each continent. We will focus on the ever more urgent question of climate change and human destruction of the natural world. We will ask what the BBC's production teams experienced and uncovered in terms of the challenges species are facing around the world, and the ways they are tackling those challenges. We will also go behind the scenes through the BBC's 'making of' clips, which show the extremes that film-makers face to bring these incredible stories to life for viewers. Some incredible ‘film firsts’ were achieved in making this series, including the largest aggregation of whales ever filmed, wolves hunting in the mountains of Italy, and multiple animal interactions captured in unprecedented detail thanks to the development of smaller, quieter drones. We will interview series Executive Producer Jonny Keeling about the BBC's newly strengthened stance on climate change. We will hopefully also interview a crew member or producer (possibly via Skype/sent from location) about the experience of shooting such an ambitious and groundbreaking project. We will also select one or two success stories the series tells about species brought back from the brink: whales almost hunted out, or pumas in Patagonia which are slowly recovering now that their habitat has been protected. We will hopefully interview one of the scientists involved in one of these projects, who can tell us the story of how to save a species. The gist of the Seven Worlds One Planet series and our story will be a celebration of our natural wonders alongside an awareness of how delicate these systems are and how vital it is to preserve them.
metadata.Further information: We will shoot at the launch of the series on Saturday 7 March 2020, capturing links, an interview with EP Jonny Keeling and some visuals of guests arriving to watch the Africa episode (series finale). The other interviews are yet to be set up and will happen at a later date. In conversation with BBC it has been agreed that the insert will TX on 22 March 2020, one week before the launch of the series.
